title: Don't quarrel
hookLine: don't dispute, or you'll lose heart and your strength will go (8:46)
last: MUQALLIB AL-QULUB — HE IS NEARER THAN MY HEART.

cards: A sailboat with two people at the helm, each pulling the tiller their own way, goes nowhere. The sail flaps. The boat turns in circles.
Everyone works hard, and all the work cancels out. Families do this. Teams do this.

Whole communities do it, over things that look enormous at the time and tiny ten years later. Surah eight remembers a community that had just come through Badr, and would learn at Uhud what quarreling costs.
Its verse forty-six uses the image of wind.

teach.b: In Pickthall's words: “dispute not one with another lest ye falter and your strength depart from you; but be steadfast!” The verse adds: Allah is with the steadfast.
The Arabic word for dispute is tanaza'u, from a root that means to pull, to snatch: two people tugging the same rope in opposite directions. It's not ordinary disagreement.
Companions disagreed about strategy, meanings and rulings, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ at times let the difference stand. Tanazu' is disagreement turned into a tug-of-war.
The result: fa-tafshalu, you'll lose heart, go slack, fail. And tadhhaba rihukum.
Pickthall has your strength will depart; literally, your wind will go. In Arabic, a person's wind can mean their power, their momentum, the way English says the wind went out of their sails.
Some early commentators also took it more literally: the wind of help that blows for a people at their best.
Surah three, looking back on Uhud, describes what happened: a group lost heart, disputed over the order they'd been given, and disobeyed, and the day turned.
The archers argued over whether to hold their post on the hill, and many left it. So surah eight is naming a pattern the community would learn the hard way. Its answer isn't never disagree.
It's sabr: steadiness. Stay at your post. Hold your tongue when the argument has turned into tugging.
Allah is with the steady ones.

how: Muslim teachers cite 8:46 when calling communities, families and mosque committees to unity, and distinguish respectful scholarly difference (ikhtilaf) from divisive quarreling (tanazu').

o: never disagree with anyone about anything
don't pull against each other till your strength goes
stay silent so the enemy can't hear your plans

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: companions disagreed often. it forbids tanazu', a tug-of-war that pulls a community apart.
the Arabic for your strength will depart says, literally, your wind will go
tadhhaba rihukum: like the wind going out of your sails.
surah three links the setback at Uhud to disputing over orders
the archers argued over holding their post, and many left it.

games.q: you're one of the archers on the hill at Uhud. it looks like the battle is won, and your group starts arguing whether to stay. what did the order say?
games.why: they were told to hold their post. many left it after disputing, and the day turned (3:152).

practice: Think of one quarrel you're carrying right now: a group chat argument, a sibling standoff, a cold war with a coworker, a debate you keep replaying in the shower.
Ask honestly whether it's still a disagreement, or has become a tug-of-war. Then picture letting go of your end of the rope, just this one, and notice the slack.

wordCard.voice: Don't quarrel. Surah eight, verse forty-six: don't pull against each other, or you'll lose heart and your wind will go; be steadfast. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: and do not dispute, do not pull against one another (8:46).

carryVoice: Your line: quarrels weaken. Disagreement can stay; the tug-of-war is what drains the wind. Day four hundred nineteen, done.
